Title: Impacting Higher Education in East Africa
NewsSummary: Dr Tashmin Khamis has been unanimously elected as the President of the East African Higher Education Quality Assurance Network.
NewsContent:
​Dr Tashmin Khamis has been unanimously elected as the President of the East African Higher Education Quality Assurance Network (EAQAN).

In her new role, Dr Khamis will work closely with an 8-member executive committee drawn from the five member states of the East African Community: Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi. “I am honoured to serve the quality assurance agenda for higher education in the region and I do so proudly flying the AKU flag,” says Dr Tashmin Khamis, Director of the Network of Quality Assurance and Improvement and the Network of Teaching and Learning, set up by the AKU Office of the Provost.

EAQAN is a network of quality assurance practitioners from higher education institutions in the EAC. It works in close partnership with the Inter-University Council for East Africa (IUCEA), headquartered in Kampala, Uganda, and the various National Commissions for Higher Education such as the CUE (Kenya), TCU (Tanzania) and NCHE (Uganda). Overseas support comes from the German Rectors Conference (HRK) and DAAD (the German Academic Exchange Service).

We talked to Dr Khamis about her role as President EAQAN, its impact on higher education in the region and AKU’s standing in the education sector. 

What is EAQAN’s mandate?

EAQAN stands to promote, enhance and improve the quality of higher education in East Africa through the implementation of quality assurance (QA) activities. These include collaboration, capacity building, research and scholarship, linkages with regional and international QA bodies and hosting conferences.

What impact do you hope to have on the work of the EAQAN and higher education in East Africa?

EAQAN was set up two years ago, and we will be building on the solid grounding of the founding members to promote quality in higher education in the region. For the first time, IUCEA has committed to providing financial and other support to EAQAN to enhance the impact already seen. Some 80 universities from the EAC countries participated in the last two annual EAQAN forums. My executive committee hopes to set a strategic direction for the Network, based on an assessment of needs. Some areas already identified include the enhancement of self-assessment and peer reviews; support for promoting student-centred teaching and learning; and learning outcomes assessment.

What role does AKU hope to play in higher education in East Africa?

AKU is already viewed as a higher education institution that promotes quality. Being such a central part of the Network will enable us to have a much greater and wider impact in the enhancement of quality in the region. At the 2014 EAQAN conference in Arusha, Tanzania, AKU was acknowledged for sharing resource persons who facilitated workshops on quality teaching and learning in higher education for some 100 participants.

Additionally, AKU will also be able to influence higher education policy as the Network works closely with national higher education commissions and with the regional IUCEA, as they, too, are charged to improve quality of university education in the region. This will include three key areas that the IUCEA is currently working on: internal quality assurance; rankings and ratings of universities; and the qualifications framework to promote regional harmonization and a credit accumulation transfer system.

As AKU asserts itself as a regional university in East Africa, with the principal campus planned in Arusha, the participation at this level with EAQAN, the IUCEA and the EAC, also based in Arusha, shows our solidarity with the vision of harmonization of higher education in this region.
